title: The month of Chet
hook: in Chet, remember the Lord and great joy comes (Barah Maha, ang 133)

segments.voice: Yesterday, veechhurhe, and your line: unite us. Did you lay one brick back the other way? Today the year begins, with the first month and its spring. Day five hundred sixty-six.

The cold has finally gone. Mustard fields that were yellow all winter are going to seed. Wheat is turning gold and heavy, a few weeks from harvest. Trees push out new leaves overnight, and the koel, a bird with a rising call, starts singing in the mornings. This is Chet, roughly March into April in Punjab, the month when everything seems to come back. And Guru Arjan begins his year of longing here, in the season when, you'd think, nobody has any reason to long for anything.
screen: `THE COLD GONE, WHEAT GOING GOLD.` → `CHET: MARCH INTO APRIL IN PUNJAB.` → `LONGING IN THE SEASON OF PLENTY.`

segments.voice: Chet is the first month in Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, and the Nanakshahi calendar begins its year with Chet too. The stanza on ang 133 opens, in paraphrase: in Chet, by worshiping the Lord of the universe, a deep and lasting joy arises. Then it says how. Meeting the holy ones, the One is found, and the tongue repeats the Name. Those who have found their Lord, their coming into the world is counted. To live even a moment without the One is to waste a life. The One is present in water, on land, in the sky, and in the forests. And for those who don't keep the One in mind, how much pain they suffer. The stanza closes with a wish: I touch the feet of whoever brings me to meet that Lord in Chet. Notice the joy. It's not the joy of the season itself, the sunshine and the new leaves. It's the joy of remembering. The spring is everywhere, the stanza says, in water and land and sky and forest, because the One is everywhere in it. So the green outside becomes a reminder of what's inside it. Some Punjabi listeners also hear a play of sounds here. Chet is the month, but chet is also an everyday word for awareness, for keeping something in mind, as in chete, remembering. The stanza never says it's a pun, so it's only a sound worth noticing: the month of Chet, and the work of chet, remembering. In the season when the world wakes up, the soul is asked to wake up too.
screen: `CHET: THE FIRST MONTH.` · `JOY FROM REMEMBERING THE ONE.` · `WATER, LAND, SKY AND FOREST.` · `CHET, AND CHET: REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `CHET: JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plant something in spring. Whatever month it is where you are, you can do a small version. Sit and picture a seed: what you'd plant, where, how deep. If you have a pot, a seed, or even a kitchen scrap like a green onion root, plan to put it in soil or water today. As you picture it, breathe slowly and think of one thing in you that's been waiting to grow. Let the seed hold that wish. If you pray, you can say Waheguru over it. The bell holds the time.
Chet. Spring, the first month of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha: remembering the One brings deep joy, and the One fills water, land, sky and forest.
Your line: chet: joy. Today, plant your seed, and each time you see something green, let it remind you to remember. Day five hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: On the sangrand of Chet, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Chet stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, and in the Nanakshahi calendar Chet is the first month of the year.

original.note: Gurmukhi: in Chet, the spring month; the stanza's first word.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spring poem.
what it means: the joy of Chet is the joy of remembering the One, who fills all the green of spring.
what a scholar hears: Chet opens the Majh Barah Maha; chet is also everyday Punjabi for awareness and remembering, though the text never names it a pun.
